_: CAMP-56. The record of who read our legal pages before they went live. See scripts/seo/check-legal-review.mjs. While `acknowledgedUntil` is in the future a public build warns; past it, it fails. That is the same shape as known-advisories.json: a debt we have looked at, with a date it stops being acceptable.
jurisdiction: Belgium — Wetboek van economisch recht, plus GDPR and Directive 2011/83/EU. The company is UTD BV, Antwerpen.
reviewedBy: Claude (Anthropic), acting for the owner — NOT a lawyer. See `note`.
note:
WHAT THIS RECORD CLAIMS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT.

Who read these pages. Not a lawyer. On 27.10.2026 the owner decided there would be no lawyer on this project — there is no budget for one — and that this review would be done by me. This record is not legal advice and does not replace it. It asserts exactly one thing: every statement on these pages was checked against the code, and wherever the two disagreed, the page or the code was changed.

What was checked, and how. On 02.11.2026 six pages were read for the first time and thirteen discrepancies were found between text and code; three more of the same kind turned up afterwards in places the first pass had not listed. All are closed. The pages no longer promise to accept photographs and reviews the code does not accept; no longer call one browser key the only one when there are three; no longer claim a tick-box confirming age that does not exist; no longer say "we hold the following, and nothing else" while listing what we do not hold. Each checked statement now has a test that turns red when the code and the text drift apart, and every one of those tests was proved by mutation.

WHAT THIS RECORD DOES NOT CLAIM.
- That the wording is optimal under Belgian law. It is TRUE; that is a different thing.
- That the list of processors will stay complete. It is complete on this date and is held by a test.
- That Article 28 contracts exist with every processor. With Hetzner, yes, concluded 02.11.2026. With Cloudflare, NOT CHECKED — the register says so in those words.
- That the pages were checked against the national law of other member states, beyond what follows directly from the GDPR and Directive 2011/83/EU.

When this record stops applying. By itself, the moment any named page's version is raised: the guard compares versions, not names. That is deliberate — what was read was a specific text, not "the terms" in general.

Why the acknowledgement runs only three months. This review was done by a non-lawyer. Law moves, our reading of it ages, and a record that sits unquestioned for a year stops being a review and becomes a habit. Three months is short enough that somebody has to look again while the reasons for each decision are still recoverable from this repository.

ATTRIBUTION 1.1, added 02.11.2026 (#394). 1.0 named five of the thirty-eight sources the site actually shows; 1.1 names all of them, each with the licence read from the licensor's own page, not from a summary. Two guards hold it: a hand-written list of the files where sources are defined, and — because a hand-written list sees only what is written in it — a sweep of every production file (603 files, 103 hosts on the day), which demands that each host found be named on the page, be a reference link, or carry a written exception with a reason and the files it covers.

What 1.1 does NOT claim.
- That every one of the sixty-six exceptions was independently verified. Twelve were sampled; the rest rest on the stated reason, which the guard requires but cannot judge.
- That the EEA air-quality line was re-read from the catalogue itself. It was carried over from 1.0 and not re-checked against the source.
- That naming a licence is the same as meeting its conditions over time. One condition is still open by design: Open-Meteo's free tier is for non-commercial use, and the obligation to move to a paid plan is triggered by the first affiliate link on the site, which does not exist yet. The page states the licence; it is not a statement that the trigger has been handled.

PRIVACY 2.5, added 03.11.2026 (CAMP-436). CAMP-51 gave the site a new category of personal data — which account asked to claim which campsite — and the Article 30 register gained §11 the same day while this policy did not. The guard that compares code with the register cannot see that gap: it reads the register, not the policy. 2.5 closes it with a section that states what the record holds (a hash of the code, a MASK of the address, never the address itself), that the letter goes to a third party who did not ask for it and does not name the person asking, that it carries a code rather than a link, the two daily limits, and the one-month term for a request nobody confirmed. Every number in it was taken from the code it describes — `spot-claim.ts` for the limits, `RULES` in retention-purge.mjs for the term, the CHECK constraint on `spot_claims` for the mask — and from register §11, which carries the same numbers in the same words.

WHAT 2.5 DOES NOT CLAIM. That the other five pages were read again on this date. They were not: their versions did not move, the review of 02.11.2026 stands for them unchanged, and `acknowledgedUntil` is left where it was rather than extended — extending it would be claiming a re-reading that did not happen. The next full pass is still due before 02.02.2027.

ATTRIBUTION 1.1 → 1.2, read 08.11.2026. The page gained a Flags section: 28 SVG files from flag-icons by Panayiotis Lipiridis, MIT, Copyright (c) 2013, vendored into apps/web/public/flags/. MIT requires the notice and the copyright to travel with the files; this page carries both, publicly, and that satisfies it. What this read actually caught, and why it was not a formality: the first draft of the section claimed the licence text sat beside the files. The owner then decided 08.11.2026 that third-party rights live in ONE place — this page — and the file beside the flags was removed. The sentence was corrected; a legal page asserting a fact that is no longer true is worse than no sentence. Nothing else on the page changed.

COOKIES 1.1 → 1.2 and PRIVACY 2.5 → 2.6, read 10.11.2026 (CAMP-448). The header gained a light/dark switch, and with it the code began writing a FOURTH entry into browser storage — `camptribe.theme`. Both pages stated, in words and in a number, «Our own code writes three entries into your browser’s storage, and nothing else». That sentence became false the moment the button shipped.

This was not caught by reading. The guard `legal-storage-surfaces.spec.tsx` reads EVERY `.setItem(` under apps/web/src and demands the same list on both pages; it went red before the feature was finished, and the first draft of the switch wrote a key (`ct-theme`) that no page named at all. Both pages now name the fourth entry, say what it holds (one word, «light» or «dark»), that it is absent until the reader presses the button, that returning to the system setting removes it, and why it needs no consent — the reader asked for it by pressing the button and the request cannot be met without remembering the answer, which is the same strictly-necessary argument already carried by `camptribe.consent`.

WHAT THIS READ DOES NOT CLAIM.
- That the strictly-necessary argument would survive a regulator who reads it differently. It is the honest reading of ePrivacy Art. 5(3) for a preference the reader set themselves, and it is the same argument this record already carries for the consent key — not a new one.
- That the other five pages were read again. They were not: their versions did not move.
- `acknowledgedUntil` is NOT extended. Extending it would claim a re-reading of everything that did not happen; the next full pass is still due before 02.02.2027.

ATTRIBUTION 1.2 → 1.3, read 11.11.2026 (CAMP-484). The page told the reader that height above sea level was «reached through Open-Meteo's elevation endpoint at api.open-meteo.com». After CAMP-484 that is no longer the path: the HTTP call was deleted from apps/api/src/osm/compute-context.ts and the figures are now read from the `openmeteo` bucket on AWS Open Data. 1.3 names the bucket AND the host the files are actually read from (openmeteo.s3.amazonaws.com), keeps Open-Meteo as the licensor, and adds the one sentence the old text never carried — how the relief figure is actually computed (highest minus lowest across eight points on a one-kilometre circle plus the centre).

WHY THIS IS A CORRECTION AND NOT AN EDIT. An attribution page is a statement about where data comes from. Leaving a route we no longer travel is telling the reader an untruth on the one page that promises accuracy.

WHAT THIS READ DOES NOT CLAIM.
- That the licence changed. It did not: both the endpoint and the bucket carry CC BY 4.0, and the letter from Open-Meteo (Ticket#235498, 10.11.2026) lifted OUR restriction — it confirmed the bucket is usable commercially — rather than changing theirs.
- That the non-commercial trigger noted under 1.1 is resolved. It is narrower now: it concerned the free API, which this change removes from the code entirely. The free API is no longer called from anywhere in apps/api.
- That the other six pages were read again. They were not; their versions did not move.
- `acknowledgedUntil` is NOT extended. The next full pass is still due before 02.02.2027.

ATTRIBUTION 1.3 → 1.4, read 11.11.2026 (CAMP-469). The page gained a «Decorative images» section: the banners are AI-generated, with FLUX1.1 [pro] ultra from Black Forest Labs, through fal.run, from a text prompt alone (no picture supplied), we keep the prompt and seed of each, and none shows a real place. Six statements, set out in five paragraphs because model and host are checked together, each against the code or the files and not against the text of the page:
1. Model and host. `scripts/images/generate-banners.mjs` sets MODEL to `fal-ai/flux-pro/v1.1-ultra` and POSTs to `https://fal.run/${MODEL}`; the link on the page is the same URL. CONFIRMED.
2. «From a text prompt alone, no picture supplied». The request body carries exactly: prompt, aspect_ratio, num_images, seed, raw, safety_tolerance, enable_safety_checker, output_format. No image_url, image_prompt, init_image or any other input image, in the file now or in either of its two revisions in git (grep over the full history of the file: 0 hits). The fal model page says the model ACCEPTS optional reference images; this script does not send one. CONFIRMED for the script. NOT proved: that the four committed .webp files were produced by exactly this revision — the generation ran on a machine that is not this repository.
3. «We keep the prompt and seed of every image». `docs/image-sources.md` holds the prompt and the seed of all four, and each is byte-identical to what `generate-banners.mjs --dry-run` prints. CONFIRMED.
4. «They show no real place». All four files were looked at one by one on 11.11.2026: a lone tent in a misty meadow; a night sky over a dark forest edge; a white van seen from behind on a straight empty road between fields; a lit orange tent in a clearing with spruce behind. No landmark, sign, lettering, flag or building was found, and no place I could name. The van has a plate recess with a faint pale-yellow rectangle, with no readable character. CONFIRMED as far as eyes go; see below for what that does not mean.
5. «The banners behind page headings and on the section cards are AI-generated». TRUE OF THE FILES, NOT YET OF WHAT A READER SEES ON THIS BRANCH. At the commit this was read at, `apps/web/src` references the .webp files from 0 files and the old hand-drawn .svg from 9. The component swap is a separate change (`docs/image-sources.md`, «Not in scope here»). The record is written for the page as it will stand once that swap has shipped; shipping the migration BEFORE the swap would put a sentence on the page that is false for as long as the gap lasts.

WHAT THE TERMS SAY, read by curl on 11.11.2026 and not recalled.
- fal.ai Terms of Service, «Last Updated: September 8, 2026» (fal.ai/legal/terms-of-service). They contain NO sentence granting or assigning the customer any right in the Output Content. What they do say: «Customer owns and retains all right, title, and interest in and to the Customer Input»; «Output Content may not be unique across users»; «Company does not represent, warrant, or covenant that any Output Content will be original, will not infringe rights of any third party (including intellectual property rights)»; «Customer's Confidential Information includes Customer Input and Output Content generated for Customer»; the right to use the Services is for «your own personal or internal business use». Whether commercial use of the Output is permitted is therefore NOT STATED in fal's terms. The model page at fal.ai carries a label, «License: Commercial use enabled via fal partnership»; that is a one-line label, with no text and no link to one, and is not treated here as a licence.
- Black Forest Labs Developer Terms of Service, «Last Revised on August 4, 2026» (bfl.ai/legal/developer-terms-of-service), §4(b): «As between you and us, we claim no ownership rights in and to your Output … You and your End Users may use Outputs for your or their own personal or commercial purposes, subject to any restrictions set forth in these Terms or applicable law.» §3(b): «As between you and us, you own all right, title, and interest in and to Output.» Its website Terms say the same in fewer words («We claim no ownership rights in and to Your Content»). These are BFL's contract with whoever contracts with BFL. We contract with fal, not with BFL. Nothing I read says those terms pass through to a customer of fal, and nothing says they do not. NOT ESTABLISHED.
- One BFL restriction that may touch us: Developer Terms forbid «Remove, disable, alter, obscure, any Content Credentials» (C2PA provenance metadata). The script re-encodes the model's JPEG to webp with sharp; none of the four committed files contains a C2PA/JUMBF marker. I did not call the API, so I do not know whether fal's response carried credentials in the first place. NOT ESTABLISHED either way.
- Also not resolved: fal's Terms forbid «develop[ing] any scripts or software applications that interact with or integrate with the Services unless first authorized in writing», while another clause permits API access through a «Customer Solution». I could not reconcile the two from the text; this script is a script that calls the API.
So the honest summary is: BFL's own terms, where they apply, allow commercial use of Output; fal's terms, which are the ones we actually accepted, are SILENT on it; whether BFL's pass through is NOT ESTABLISHED. The page says nothing about rights in the output, and that is deliberate. `docs/image-sources.md` says «We hold the output as the party that ran the generation» — that is stronger than anything above and is NOT supported by what was read.

WHAT THIS READ DOES NOT CLAIM.
- That the banners may be used commercially. Not established, as above. It is not «permitted» and it is not «forbidden»; it is unread-to-the-end.
- That any licence document for FLUX1.1 [pro] ultra exists beyond what is quoted. I found none; the Hugging Face licence page answered 401 and was not read; the BFL self-hosted licence concerns self-hosting, which we do not do.
- That «no real place» means the pictures resemble no real place. It means none showed a landmark, sign or lettering that I could recognise. A generated meadow may look like a meadow somewhere. The page says none «is a photograph of any campsite», which is true by construction: nobody photographed anything.
- That copyright subsists in the output at all under Belgian or EU law. Not examined.
- That the terms quoted will stay as they are. They carry «Last Updated» dates of September and August 2026 and change; the quotation is of 11.11.2026.
- That the other six pages were read again. They were not: their versions did not move.
- `acknowledgedUntil` is NOT extended. Extending it would claim a re-reading of everything that did not happen; the next full pass is still due before 02.02.2027.

PRIVACY 2.6 → 2.7, read 12.11.2026 (CAMP-504). The site began COUNTING: page views of a campsite, clicks on its website and phone number, a campsite appearing in a route the planner built, and searches that found nothing together with the map filters that were on. Two sentences on the page would have become untrue without a change: that a planner request is not stored (a campsite it proposed now adds one to a daily total), and — by implication — that nothing here measures use. 2.7 adds one section («Counting what is looked at»), a line in «The trip planner», and a line in «How long we keep it»; register §12 and §9 carry the same facts.

What the new section says, and what holds each sentence in code. Totals, one number per day, not a log: two tables, `spot_event_daily` and `zero_result_search_daily`, whose column lists a database test reads back and fails on any column outside the two lists. No IP, browser string, cookie, browser storage or search text: the same test, plus a web test that the page code touches neither cookies nor storage. The one-way hash that stops a person being counted twice lives in the server's memory for the rest of the UTC day, is written nowhere, and the class holding it is tested to import no file, network or database code. The source of a visit is one word of four and the address is discarded: a test feeds a referrer carrying a name and finds neither it nor the host in the table. The website link goes through `/out/<slug>`, which sends the reader only to the address stored for that campsite; tests put a foreign URL into eight query parameters and into the slug and get the stored address or a 404. Known crawlers are not counted. Four mutations were run on exactly these (bot filter removed, de-duplication removed, URL accepted from the query, full referrer stored instead of the class) and each turned a test red.

WHAT THIS READ DOES NOT CLAIM.
- That the legal basis (legitimate interest, Art. 6(1)(f)) would survive a regulator who reads it differently. It is the same basis the page already uses for the error and dead-link logs; no lawyer read it.
- That reading the referrer in the reader's browser and sending its host to us is outside ePrivacy Art. 5(3). The page says only what is true: nothing is STORED on the device. Whether reading `document.referrer` counts as access is not settled here.
- That nobody is counted twice. After a server restart, or on a second node, the same person can be counted again; the page says so.
- That copying coordinates, downloading GPX or «showing» a phone number are measured. The site has no such buttons yet and shows the number always; the page says the first two are not offered, and the register says what is counted instead (a click on the number).
- That the totals have a deletion date. They have none, and the page says that is because they hold no personal data. If a column about a person is ever added, that sentence becomes false and the database test goes red.
- That the other six pages were read again. They were not; their versions did not move.
- `acknowledgedUntil` is NOT extended. The next full pass is still due before 02.02.2027.

COOKIES 1.2 → 1.3 AND PRIVACY 2.7 → 2.8, read 12.11.2026 (CAMP-501). The site began remembering which of two readers is looking: «I have a camper» or «I am renting one», two buttons in the header, kept in the browser's local storage as `camptribe.persona`. Both pages state the list of entries by name and by number («four … and nothing else»); with a fifth key in the code that sentence would have been untrue on the page that exists to be true, so each page gains one entry and the number becomes five. Nothing else on either page changed.

What the new entry says, and what holds each sentence in code. One word, «owner» or «renter», never sent to us: the key is written only by the button handler (`components/persona-toggle.tsx`) and read only by a script in the page head that copies it onto the <html> element; neither makes a request. No entry until the reader presses a button, and pressing the same button again removes it: a browser test presses, reloads, opens another page, and reads the key back; another presses twice and finds the key gone. A stored value that is neither word is ignored: a unit test runs the real head script over a fake store holding «admin», an empty string and nothing, and over a store that throws. The consent argument is the one already on the pages for the theme choice: the reader asked for it by pressing, and the thing asked for (the page putting first what that choice asks for) cannot be delivered without remembering the answer. The guard that reads every `.setItem(` under `apps/web/src` and compares the list with both pages went red on the new key before the pages were changed (ten tests red in the unit run, six of them these) and green after. Five mutations were run on the behaviour (save removed, head script reading another key, the rule that hides the rental block for owners, a home card losing its marker, the pinned heading unpinned) and each turned a test red.

WHAT THIS READ DOES NOT CLAIM.
- That the consent reasoning would survive a regulator who reads «strictly necessary» narrowly. It is the same reasoning the pages already use for the theme choice; no lawyer read it.
- That the other five pages were read again. They were not; their versions did not move.
- That anything about the entry is known for a reader whose browser blocks storage: the choice then lasts until the page is reloaded, and the pages do not describe that case.
- `acknowledgedUntil` is NOT extended. The next full pass is still due before 02.02.2027.
